title: True or false: what a container is
prompt: A teammate is writing an onboarding doc for notes-api and asks you to review five claims about containers. Select **every** statement that is correct.
hints: Ask of each claim: is this about what a process can see, what it can use, or what's on its disk?
Namespaces are about visibility; cgroups are about resource limits.
Three of the five are correct.
explanation: Containers are host processes that share the host kernel, which is why they start fast and why isolation is weaker than a VM. Each container gets its own writable layer on top of the shared read-only image, and one image can back any number of containers. Docker on Linux does not create a VM per container, and cgroups limit resource *use*; it's namespaces that control what a process can *see*.

shared-kernel.text: Every container on a Linux host uses the same kernel as the host.
shared-kernel.why: Correct. There is no guest kernel. That is the source of both the speed and the weaker isolation.

own-writable.text: Each container gets its own writable layer; changes there vanish when the container is removed.
own-writable.why: Correct. That's why data that must survive goes in a volume.

vm-each.text: Docker creates a small virtual machine for each container so they can't affect each other.
vm-each.why: Not on Linux. Docker Desktop uses one shared VM on macOS and Windows, but containers inside it are still processes on one kernel.

cgroups-see.text: cgroups decide which files and processes a container is allowed to see.
cgroups-see.why: That's namespaces. cgroups cap and account for CPU, memory and I/O.

image-many.text: One image can be the template for many running containers at once.
image-many.why: Correct. Scaling to six replicas means six containers from one image.
